threads.body: `shouldStart()` can suppress the next message’s process span when a prior tracing iterator left its process scope current (for example, code called `next()` on the last item without a final `hasNext()`). The analogous Kafka and SQS tracing iterators intentionally start unconditionally so a new process span replaces that leaked context; otherwise subsequent work remains attached to the stale span. Start the process instrumenter unconditionally here as well.

replies.body: Addressed by removing SimpleConsumer process-span creation and deleting the tracing iterator/list. SimpleConsumer now emits receive CLIENT spans only, so there is no iterator-held process scope to leak.

threads.body: Extending `ArrayList` means standard traversal APIs such as `stream()`/`parallelStream()` use `ArrayList.spliterator()`, and `listIterator()` uses its own iterator; neither reaches the overridden `iterator()`. Applications processing received messages through those common APIs therefore emit no process spans. Route all traversal methods through tracing wrappers (or use a delegating `List`) and cover these paths.

replies.body: Addressed by removing the tracing list and all traversal-created process spans. The vendor's original `List` is now returned unchanged, and SimpleConsumer emits receive CLIENT spans only.

threads.body: This stable-mode success test only runs in `testMessagingPreview`, which always enables experimental receive telemetry; the default task uses legacy semconv. Add coverage for stable messaging semconv with receive telemetry disabled, verifying that SimpleConsumer still emits process spans but emits neither the new receive span nor the low-level receive span—the configuration behavior called out by this PR is otherwise untested.

replies.body: Added stable messaging coverage with receive telemetry disabled, verifying that a successful SimpleConsumer receive emits neither the new receive span nor the low-level receive span. Process spans were intentionally removed because the returned `List` provides no reliable processing-completion boundary.
